clinicalPearls: Factor H is the major fluid-phase and surface regulator of the alternative complement pathway; its deficiency leads to uncontrolled complement activation and secondary consumption of C3.
Complete deficiency and dysfunctional variants classically cause C3 glomerulopathy, including dense deposit disease, and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
A persistently low C3 with a normal or near-normal C4 reflects selective alternative-pathway consumption and is an important clue.
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome from factor H abnormalities presents with microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury, often without a diarrhoeal prodrome.
There is also an increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms owing to depletion of C3.
Variants in the factor H gene and anti-factor-H autoantibodies both cause functional deficiency and must be sought.
Complement-directed therapy, particularly terminal-pathway blockade, has transformed management of factor H-related atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
Factor H genetic variation is also strongly linked to age-related macular degeneration, illustrating the breadth of its regulatory role.
reference.pathophysiology: Factor H is the principal regulator of the alternative complement pathway, acting both in the fluid phase and on host cell surfaces. It accelerates decay of the alternative-pathway C3 convertase and serves as a cofactor for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b, thereby protecting host tissues from complement attack. When factor H is deficient or dysfunctional, the alternative pathway is left unchecked, so C3 is continuously activated and consumed, depleting circulating C3 and depositing complement on host surfaces. Endothelial injury from unregulated complement drives thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome), while glomerular C3 deposition produces C3 glomerulopathy. The accompanying fall in C3 also impairs opsonisation, adding a susceptibility to encapsulated-organism infection.
additionalInvestigations: C3 and C4 levels (typically low C3 with preserved C4)
Factor H antigenic level and functional activity
Genetic testing of CFH and related complement regulator genes
Renal function, blood film for schistocytes, haptoglobin and platelet count
Renal biopsy for C3 glomerulopathy or thrombotic microangiopathy
Assessment for encapsulated-organism infection and vaccination status
redFlags: Microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
Rapidly declining renal function or oligo-anuria
reference.prognosis: Factor H-related atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome carries a high risk of progression to end-stage renal disease and of recurrence after transplantation, though outcomes have improved substantially with complement-blocking therapy; C3 glomerulopathy tends to follow a chronic progressive course.
pitfalls: Overlooking a complement regulatory defect in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome without a diarrhoeal prodrome.
Missing anti-factor-H autoantibodies as a treatable cause of functional deficiency.
Interpreting a low C3 with normal C4 as nonspecific rather than a marker of alternative-pathway dysregulation.
Proceeding to renal transplantation without recognising the high recurrence risk.
Neglecting infection prophylaxis when C3 is depleted.
references: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice, current edition
Oxford Textbook of Medicine, current edition
Reviews on complement regulation, C3 glomerulopathy and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
management: Terminal complement inhibition with an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody (eculizumab or ravulizumab) as the mainstay for atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
Plasma exchange or plasma infusion in acute thrombotic microangiopathy to supply functional factor H and remove autoantibody
Vaccination against encapsulated organisms, especially meningococcus, before complement inhibition, with antibiotic prophylaxis on treatment
Supportive renal care including dialysis for acute kidney injury and blood pressure control
Monitoring of C3, haemolysis markers and renal function, and surveillance for relapse
Nephrology referral with careful peri-transplant planning given the high recurrence risk, and consideration of combined liver-kidney transplantation
Genetic counselling and family screening for CFH variants
